what: Atlantic Union Bankshares is a bank in Virginia. It takes deposits and lends across Virginia, Maryland and North Carolina, serving businesses, financing commercial property and writing residential mortgages, with wealth management alongside.
customers: Small and mid-sized businesses, commercial property owners, homeowners and retail depositors across the mid-Atlantic, plus wealth management clients.
money: The spread between interest earned on loans and paid on deposits.
Wealth management, service charges and other banking fees.
moat: A bank’s durable advantage is a base of low-cost deposits from customers who do not move, built over decades in specific communities. Atlantic Union has that across Virginia, and recent acquisitions have extended the footprint. Local lending relationships are the other asset, and neither can be bought quickly.
risks: Commercial real estate is the sector’s main concern and is a meaningful share of the loan book.
Recent acquisitions mean integrating another bank’s deposits and inheriting its credit decisions, which is where bank acquisitions go wrong.
Results depend on interest rates set by the Federal Reserve rather than on management decisions.
The jump in revenue from $817.4M in 2024 to $1.4B in 2025 reflects acquisitions rather than organic growth, which makes trends hard to read.
Eight analysts average a $45.63 target, about 23% above the current price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 10.0 times earnings, 7.3 times EV/EBITDA and 9.5 times free cash flow.
Trailing net income of $519.9M on $1.6B of revenue, with free cash flow of $549.0M.
Cash of $966.5M against $890.8M of holding company debt is a balanced position.
Virginia and the mid-Atlantic have stable, government-linked economies that produce steady credit experience.
Scale from acquisitions improves the cost structure, which in banking is one of the few durable advantages.
watch: Non-performing loans and the commercial real estate composition. Credit is the only thing that turns a good banking year into a disaster, and it is visible before it is fatal.
view: Atlantic Union has grown by buying other Virginia banks, and that is both the opportunity and the thing to examine. Bank acquisitions work when they add low-cost deposits and cut duplicated costs, and they fail when the acquirer inherits credit decisions it did not make and did not understand. The revenue jump from $817 million to $1.4 billion is acquisition arithmetic rather than organic growth, which makes every trend in the financial statements harder to read than it should be.

The underlying franchise is sound. Virginia and the mid-Atlantic have unusually stable economies, heavily influenced by federal government employment and contracting, which produces steady credit experience through cycles that hurt more volatile regions. Deposits from customers who have banked locally for decades are the real asset, and they are not available for purchase except by buying the bank that holds them.

At 10 times earnings and 7.3 times EV/EBITDA the price is modest, and $966 million of cash against $891 million of holding company debt is a reasonable structure. Scale from the acquisitions should improve the cost ratio, which in banking is one of very few durable advantages — a bank with lower costs can out-earn a larger competitor indefinitely.

What I would watch is the credit coming across in the acquisitions, specifically commercial real estate. Those losses emerge slowly: a loan does not default until it matures and cannot be refinanced at current rates, so the picture takes two or three more years of maturities to clarify. An acquirer is particularly exposed here, because the loans were underwritten by somebody else to somebody else’s standards. Non-performing loans, broken down by what came from where, is the disclosure worth hunting for.
bull: Acquisition scale cuts the cost ratio while stable mid-Atlantic deposits fund steady lending, and 10 times earnings proves conservative.
bear: Acquired commercial real estate loans turn out worse than underwritten, losses emerge as they mature, and integration costs compound the damage.
